home.h1: Before the AI says “done,” make it try the thing itself
lead: pstack is a free, open-source set of work rules you install into your AI. With it, the AI first makes sure it knows what you want, then changes only what needs changing.
You don't need to know how to code
home.ctaNote: The beginner track is three lessons, 20 minutes.
PAIN: The AI says “done!” You open it, and the button does nothing.
You say “still broken.” It says “sorry, fixed now.” Same result, again and again.
You wanted one small change, and it changed a pile of things you never asked about.
DIFF: Starts without checking what you want
Repeats your goal in its own words first, so you can correct it right away
Changes things somewhere that looks about right
Figures out the problem first, then changes as little as it can
Lists what it actually checked and what it saw, and says plainly what it couldn't check
home.lessonsP: Read them in order, 20 minutes in all. After these three you can use it. Everything else on the site is for looking up later.
YES: You've made small pages, plug-ins or tools with AI and been burned by “done” that wasn't
You already have Claude Code (or Cursor or Codex) and can chat with the AI in it
You'd rather get it right than get it fast
NO: You haven't used a tool like Claude Code yet: install it with the official guide first, and come back once you can chat
It's a tiny change like a typo or a color: just ask the AI directly
You only want fastest and cheapest: pstack checks more, so it's slower and uses more of your plan
home.devP: pstack is the pack of skills poteto (formerly on the React core team; wrote pstack at Cursor, now builds Grok Bot) uses for their own code every day: 35 skills, 22 playbooks and 24 engineering principles. Below are the four steps it takes for every task, and the 9-step full guide.
FLOW: The goal, plus how you'll know it's done. For example: “reproduce it first, then fix, then verify.”
It chooses one of 22 playbooks and copies its steps into the todo list as they are.
/how to read code, /architect to settle a design, /interrogate to pick holes; subagents when there's a lot to do.
Real command output, screenshots, before-and-after. If something can't be verified, it says so.
